the first fifteen verses praise the Buddha’s form-body (rūpakāya), and the subsequent five verses, beginning with "All those of the past," praise the Buddha’s name-body (nāmakāya).

Within this praise of the form body (*rūpakāya*), the first verse offers a reverent general eulogy; the next thirteen verses provide specific praises according to his virtues; and the final verse concludes with a praise of its boundlessness.

This is the opening section. The first line sets forth that which is worthy of praise; the second line indicates the dwelling place of the one being praised; the third line expresses homage through the three types of action (*trikarma*).
As for "to arrive" (*zhì*), it means to be focused or single-minded.
"Sincerity" (cheng) means reality.
"Investigation" (ji) means reaching the ultimate.
"Head" (shou) means the top of the body.
Because one brings the head to the ground, it is called "prostrating with the head" (kai-shou).
"Ritual" (li) means reverence.
Now, this applies to all three karmas; it is not merely the ritual of the head, for by citing the physical action, the mental and verbal actions are also manifested.
Focusing the mind upon an object is termed "one-pointedness of mind" (*ekāgratā*); it does not refer to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*) or the like.

A single phrase that expresses praise is called a "laudatory eulogy" (*praśamsā*), while praising by extolling the virtues of something in relation to its specific functions is called a "hymn" (*stuti*).
Sūtra: “‘The Unsurpassed, Pure, Honored Muni, his bodily radiance shines like gold.
Commentary: The following is a specific praise according to his qualities.
Regarding the praises, there are mixed praises of the marks and the excellences; they are called "mixed" because the excellences follow upon the marks.
There are sixteen such praises: eleven praise the marks and five praise the excellences.
This first half-verse praises the physical marks, specifically that the skin of the fourteen parts of the body is golden in color.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, fascicle 381, states: "The Buddha spoke to Subhūti concerning the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs. All subsequent passages should be understood according to this principle.

It is said: "Fourteenth, the skin of the World-Honored One’s body is entirely of a true golden color, brilliant and radiant like a sublime golden pedestal, adorned with various jewels and a delight to all."
Or it may be a praise of the body’s constant radiance.
As the Sūtra says: "The most supreme among all sounds, like the resonance of Great Brahmā or the roll of thunder."
The commentary states:
The second praise concerns the twenty-seven marks of the Brahma-voice.
As the sutra says: "The World-Honored One’s Brahma-voice is harmonious and elegant in its diction and rhythm; whether the assembly is large or small, all hear it equally."
The resonance of his voice vibrates like a celestial drum, and his speech is elegant and refined like the song of the kalaviṅka bird.
The Sūtra says: “The color of his hair is like that of a king of black bees; it is coiled and spiraled with a deep blue-black luster.”
The commentary states:
This third [verse] praises the excellence of the hair.
As the Sūtra says: "The World-Honored One’s hair on his head is long and deep blue-black; it is dense and never white."
Sūtra: “‘The teeth are white, even, and closely set like white jade or snow; they are level, upright, and manifest with radiance.
Commentary: This is the fourth praise, concerning the mark of the teeth.
As the Sūtra says: "The Blessed One has forty teeth, which are even, level, clean, closely set, deep-rooted, and whiter than white jade or snow. And the Sūtra says:
"His eyes are pure and stainless, exquisitely beautiful, like the broad petals of a great blue lotus; his tongue is wide and long, exceedingly soft, like a red lotus emerging from the water."
Commentary: The fifth praise concerns the marks [of the Buddha].
As the Sūtra says: "Twenty-ninth, the World-Honored One’s eyes are deep blue-black with a bright white sclera, adorned with a red ring, pure and clearly distinct."
The sixth is the mark of the tongue, as stated in the Sūtra: "Twenty-sixth, the World-Honored One’s tongue-mark is pure, broad, and long; it can cover the face up to the hairline and the ears."

Sūtra: "Between his eyebrows there is always a white tuft of hair, curling to the right in a graceful spiral with the color of crystal; his eyebrows are fine, long, and shaped like the new moon, their radiant hue surpassing that of the king of bees."
Commentary: The seventh [verse] praises the thirty-first mark, the eyebrows; the eighth praises the thirty-ninth excellence, the eyebrows.

The Sūtra says: "The nose is high, long, and straight like a gold bar; it is pure, wondrous, lustrous, and its marks are flawless. When any exquisite fragrance in all the worlds is smelled, he knows exactly where it originates."
Commentary: This ninth praise concerns the minor mark of the nose.
The first half praises the excellence of its color, while the second half praises the excellence of its faculties.

Sūtra: “The World-Honored One’s most supreme body is golden in color; each pore-tip possesses a mark no different from the others. Deep blue, soft, and curling to the right in pattern, its subtle and wondrous luster is beyond comparison.”
The commentary states:
The tenth [mark] is the mark of having a single hair growing from each pore; the twelfth is the mark of having the tips of the body hairs all curling upward.

Sūtra: “At his first birth, his body was endowed with wondrous radiance that universally illumined all worlds throughout the ten directions; it was able to extinguish the suffering of sentient beings within the three realms of existence, causing them all to receive peace and happiness.”

May those in the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, as well as those among the asuras, devas, and humans, be caused to eliminate all their manifold sufferings and constantly experience natural peace and security.
"The radiance of his body’s color constantly shines everywhere, like refined gold, wondrous and beyond compare.
The commentary states:
The following two and a half verses constitute the eleventh round of praise for the mark of bodily radiance; the former is brief and the latter is detailed.
This section is divided into three parts:
first, half a verse on the body-light illuminating the environment;
second, one and a half verses praising the benefits of the body-light, within which the first half provides a general summary and the subsequent verse provides a detailed explanation.
The latter half of the verse reveals that his radiance is peerless.

The Sūtra says: “His face is perfectly bright like the full moon; the color of his lips is as beautiful as the *bimba* fruit; his gait and deportment resemble those of a lion; and the brilliance of his body’s light is like the rising sun.”
The commentary states:
In twelve characters, one phrase praises the World-Honored One’s mark of the full moon-like countenance; the mark of his eyebrows is pure and brilliant, like the bow of the Heavenly Emperor.
The eyebrows and face are divided into two parts, which also include three of the marks of excellence on the face.

Verse thirteen praises the Buddha’s excellent color of his lips; verse fourteen, in its first half, praises the Buddha’s seventh mark of excellence: that his gait proceeds straight forward like that of an elephant king.

Eighth, his gait is majestic and solemn like that of a lion; ninth, his gait is steady and level like that of a bull-king; tenth, his gait is elegant and refined like that of a swan-king—these comprise the totality of his walking.
Sūtra: “‘His arms and forearms are slender and long, reaching past his knees; their appearance is like hanging branches of the sāla tree. Commentary:
This is the fifteenth praise, the ninth mark of the Buddha’s arms.

Sūtra: “A halo one fathom wide illuminates the boundless, its brilliance like that of a hundred thousand suns; it reaches everywhere throughout all Buddha-fields, awakening the deluded according to their conditions wherever they may be.”
Commentary: The final three verses consist of sixteen praises of the Buddha’s twenty-second mark, that of the World-Honored One whose constant radiance extends one fathom on each side of his face.
This section is divided into three parts:

The first verse concerns the light illuminating according to conditions; the second verse concerns the extinguishing of all suffering of birth; and the third verse concerns the ability to bestow happiness.
This is the first [section].
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "The light from the Tathāgata’s body spontaneously illuminates the trichiliocosm, while through intentional focus, it can illuminate infinite worlds."
Out of compassion for sentient beings, he gathers light that constantly illuminates each face to a distance of one *vyāma*.
Thus, whether contracting or expanding according to conditions, he acts solely to benefit all beings.

The Sūtra says: “The net of pure radiance is beyond compare; its flowing brilliance fills hundreds of thousands of worlds. It shines universally throughout the ten directions without obstruction, and all darkness is entirely dispelled.”
The commentary states:
This refers to the removal of the suffering of birth.
Just as Śakra’s net transforms sentient beings, so too is the bodily radiance of the World-Honored One.

Sūtra: “The compassionate light of the Sugata bestows happiness; its wondrous color is translucent and equal to a mountain of gold. Its flowing radiance reaches hundreds of thousands of lands, and all sentient beings who encounter it attain liberation.”
Commentary: Bestowing happiness.
The Buddha’s compassion arises; this is called the compassionate light of the Sugata.
There are two types of giving joy:
first, worldly joy;
and that which pertains to all who have renounced, namely supramundane joy, because "renunciation" refers to nirvana.

Sūtra: “The Buddha’s body has accomplished immeasurable merit; adorned by all virtues, it transcends the triple world and alone is called supreme. It is the most excellent in the world, with nothing equal to it.”
The commentary states:
The final verse concludes the boundless praise.
Since the primary and secondary marks (lakṣaṇa-vyañjana) constitute the portion of merit, they are called "immeasurable merit."
Because it is untainted (*anāsrava*), it transcends the three realms.
Because it is utterly perfect, there is nothing equal to it.

The Sūtra says: "All Buddhas of the past, as numerous as the atoms of the great earth; and the Honored Ones of the ten directions in the future and present, likewise as many as the multitude of atoms of the great earth."
The commentary states:
The following five verses praise the *nāmakāya* (name-body).
The aforementioned *rūpakāya* (form-body) may also be called the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body), and this *nāmakāya* may also be called the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
This section is divided into three parts:
first, one verse describing the boundlessness of the Buddha; second, one verse of taking refuge and making offerings; and third, three verses of vocal praise.
This is the first part.

Sūtra: “With my body, speech, and mind in perfect sincerity, I prostrate and take refuge in the Buddhas of the three periods of time; I praise the boundless ocean of their merits and offer all manner of fragrant flowers as worship.”
Commentary: This refers to taking refuge and making offerings. The Sūtra says:

“Even if I were to possess a thousand tongues in my mouth, and were to praise the Tathāgata for immeasurable kalpas, the inconceivable merit of the World-Honored One is most supreme, profound, and difficult to describe.”

Even if I were to possess a hundred thousand tongues and praise a single Buddha for a single merit, it would still be difficult to know even a small fraction of it; how much more so for the boundless virtues of all Buddhas?

Even if the great earth and all the heavens, up to the pinnacle of existence, were turned into a sea of water, its drops could be counted by using the tip of a hair; yet a single merit of the Buddha is exceedingly difficult to measure.
The commentary states:
These words express praise.

The first verse provides a general praise of the Tathāgata’s emergence from the path of speech; the next [verses] establish that the virtues of a single Buddha are infinite; and the final verse praises the profound depth of these virtues, surpassing all measure and number.

Sūtra: “With my body, speech, and mind, I reverently praise the boundless virtues of all Buddhas. Whatever inconceivable fruits of supreme merit there may be, I dedicate them to all sentient beings so that they may swiftly attain Buddhahood.”
Commentary: This is the second dedication. The Sūtra says:
“After that king had praised the Tathāgata, he further developed vast vows with even deeper resolve.”
The commentary states:
The subsequent section on making vows consists of fourteen verses, divided into two parts:
first, one half-verse that provides a general heading; second, thirteen and a half verses that provide specific titles.
First: The Sūtra states:

“May I, in future ages throughout immeasurable and incalculable kalpas, always see a great golden drum in my dreams, hear the sounds of its proclamation of repentance, and praise the Buddha’s merits as being like lotus flowers.”
May I realize non-arising and attain perfect enlightenment; for the Buddhas appear but once in the world, and are extremely difficult to encounter even in hundreds of thousands of kalpas.
May I constantly hear the sound of the wondrous drum in my dreams at night, and during the day, may I repent in accordance with what is appropriate.
I shall fully cultivate the six perfections to deliver all beings from the ocean of suffering, and thereafter attain unsurpassed enlightenment.
With a pure and inconceivable Buddha-field, I offer a wondrous golden drum to the Tathāgata, while praising the true merits of all Buddhas.
Because of this, I shall see Śākyamuni Buddha, who will prophesy that I shall succeed him as the Honored One among Men.

Golden Dragon and Golden Light are my sons; in the past they were my spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). In every lifetime, may they be born into my family, so that together we may receive the prophecy of unexcelled Bodhi.

If there are sentient beings without protection or refuge, wandering through the long night of saṃsāra and undergoing manifold sufferings, may I become their place of reliance in future lives, so that they may attain peace and happiness.

May the manifold sufferings of the three realms of existence be extinguished, and may all beings attain peace and happiness according to their wishes; may they cultivate bodhi in future ages, just like those who have attained Buddhahood in the past.

By the merit of this Golden Light Repentance, may the ocean of suffering be forever exhausted and all transgressions eliminated; may karmic obstructions and afflictions be entirely extinguished, and may I swiftly attain the fruit of purity.
The great ocean of merit and wisdom is boundless in measure; pure, free from defilement, and bottomless. May I attain this ocean of virtue and swiftly realize supreme, unexcelled Bodhi.

By the power of this confession of golden light, one shall obtain the pure radiance of merit; having attained this pure and wondrous light, one shall forever illumine all things with the light of wisdom.

May the radiance of my body equal that of all Buddhas, and may my merit and wisdom likewise be so; may I alone be renowned as the most honored one in all worlds, with sovereign power and majesty beyond compare.

May we transcend the ocean of suffering with outflows; may we eternally roam the ocean of unconditioned bliss; may the ocean of merit in the present remain forever full; and may the ocean of wisdom in the future be brought to perfection.
May my buddha-field transcend the three realms, its sublime merits immeasurable; may all who possess the karmic affinity be born therein together, and may they all swiftly attain pure wisdom.
Commentary: The golden drum proclaims the sound of repentance;

logically, this should have been placed later, as it is only after making offerings to the golden drum that one should then make vows. However, for the sake of literary convenience, it is explained here at the beginning.
There are eight further specific manifestations:
first, one verse on the dream of the first vow;
second, one verse on the vow to praise the Buddha’s virtues, likening him to the *utpala* lotus flower.
The three and a half verses constitute the vow for repentance through practice.
The four single-verse sections constitute the vow for cultivating various virtues, which are fourfold:
first, practicing the six perfections; second, saving sentient beings; third, vowing to attain Buddhahood; and fourth, vowing to purify the Buddha-field.
The first five verses express the aspiration to receive the prophecy of enlightenment.
Next, one verse expresses the aspiration that one’s disciples may likewise attain it.

Following that, two verses express the aspiration to benefit others; within these, the first one and a half verses seek to bring about worldly happiness, while the latter half verse seeks to bring about supramundane happiness, which—by virtue of its excellence—leads to the attainment of the great fruit.

Alternatively, the second half of the verse concerning "sentient beings of the three realms of existence" may be understood as causing them to attain the Three Vehicles by means of the phrase "according to their minds," followed by causing them to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna.
Next, six verses express vows for one's own benefit; within these, there are six parts:

the first verse expresses the vow to repent so as to eliminate hindrances and attain nirvāṇa, wherein the "ocean of suffering" refers to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), "karma" refers to the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), and "afflictions" refer to the obstacle of delusion (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
Next, one verse prays for the attainment of the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* to achieve great enlightenment, thereby attaining the *saṃbhogakāya*;
next, one verse prays for the attainment of bodily wisdom whose light illuminates others, giving rise to the *nirmāṇakāya*;
and next, one verse prays that the light of one’s bodily wisdom may equal that of all Buddhas.

The next verse prays for transcendence of the ocean of suffering and the perfection of happiness; it contains two parts: the first half-verse concerns the departure from suffering and the attainment of happiness, while the second half-verse concerns the fulfillment of merit and the perfection of wisdom.
The perfection of merit corresponds to the causal practice, while the fulfillment of wisdom corresponds to the fruit.
As Asaṅga’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Regarding the marks of merit and the marks of the wisdom of the dharmakāya, the dharmakāya [itself] and its causal and fruitional stages are distinct."
The next verse expresses the aspiration to attain a pure land and achieve buddhahood together; its meaning is clear and may be understood from the text.
The Sūtra says: “O Miaodang, you should know that King Jinnaghu (Golden Dragon Lord) once made such an aspiration; he was none other than your own self.”
"In the past there were two sons, Jinaloka and Jinaruci, who are none other than Rajatalakṣaṇa and Rajataprabha; they shall receive my prediction.
Commentary: This third major section concludes by correlating the present with the past and authorizes that they shall indeed receive the prediction.
One verse concludes and harmonizes [the teaching], and one verse grants the prediction.
Sūtra: Upon hearing this discourse, the great assembly all resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta, vowing that in the present and the future they would always rely upon this confession.
The fourth major section below: The assembly hears [the teaching], arouses the aspiration for enlightenment, and vows to rely upon it for practice and study.
*Sūtra of the Golden Light, the Supreme King*, Commentary, Fascicle Four, Part One.
